section.title: Ministry Begins in Galilee
section.sectionRationale: With John arrested, Jesus steps forward with His opening announcement, the kingdom of God is near, and begins to gather a people. He calls fishermen, teaches with startling authority, drives out an unclean spirit, heals Peter's mother-in-law and a whole town, withdraws to pray, and cleanses a leper. In one packed day and its aftermath Mark shows the arrival of the kingdom in word and power.
section.thesis: The nearness of God's reign in Jesus is proven by His authoritative word: it summons disciples, silences demons, heals the sick, and cleanses the outcast, so that the only fitting response is to repent and believe the good news.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the kingdom announced; the first disciples called; a day of authority in Capernaum; prayer and a wider mission; and the cleansing of a leper.

units.label: The kingdom announced
units.note: repent and believe the good news

verses.text: After the arrest of John, Jesus went into Galilee and proclaimed the {{euangelion|gospel}} of God.
“The time is fulfilled,” He said, “and the {{basileia|kingdom}} of God is near. Repent and {{pisteuo|believe}} in the gospel!”
As Jesus was walking beside the Sea of Galilee, He saw Simon and his brother Andrew. They were casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
“Come, follow Me,” Jesus said, “and I will make you fishers of men.”
And at once they left their nets and followed Him.
Going on a little farther, He saw James son of Zebedee and his brother John. They were in a boat, mending their nets.
Immediately Jesus called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed Him.

units.label: A day of authority in Capernaum
units.note: even the unclean spirits obey Him

verses.text: Then Jesus and His companions went to Capernaum, and right away Jesus entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and began to teach.
The people were astonished at His teaching, because He taught as one who had {{exousia|authority}}, and not as the scribes.
Suddenly a man with an unclean spirit cried out in the synagogue:
“What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us? I know who You are, the Holy One of God!”
But Jesus rebuked the spirit. “Be silent!” He said. “Come out of him!”
At this, the unclean spirit threw the man into convulsions and came out with a loud shriek.
All the people were amazed and began to ask one another, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him!”
And the news about Jesus spread quickly through the whole region of Galilee.
As soon as Jesus and His companions had left the synagogue, they went with James and John to the home of Simon and Andrew.
Simon’s mother-in-law was sick in bed with a fever, and they promptly told Jesus about her.
So He went to her, took her by the hand, and helped her up. The fever left her, and she began to serve them.
That evening, after sunset, people brought to Jesus all the sick and demon-possessed,
and the whole town gathered at the door.
And He healed many who were ill with various diseases and drove out many demons. But He would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew who He was.

units.label: Prayer and a wider mission
units.note: that is why I have come

verses.text: Early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place to pray.
Simon and his companions went to look for Him,
and when they found Him, they said, “Everyone is looking for You!”
But Jesus answered, “Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come.”
So He went throughout Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and driving out demons.
Then a leper came to Jesus, begging on his knees: “If You are willing, You can make me {{katharizo|clean}}.”
Moved with {{splanchnizomai|compassion}}, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!”
And immediately the leprosy left him, and the man was cleansed.
Jesus promptly sent him away with a stern warning:
“See that you don’t tell anyone. But go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering Moses prescribed for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.”

But the man went out and openly began to proclaim and spread the news. Consequently, Jesus could no longer enter a town in plain view, but He stayed out in solitary places. Yet people came to Him from every quarter.

euangelion.gloss: Good news, glad tidings. Jesus proclaims the good news of God: that the long-awaited reign of God has arrived in Him. It is an announcement to be believed and obeyed, calling for repentance and trust.

basileia.gloss: Kingdom, reign, kingly rule. The kingdom of God is God's saving royal power breaking into history in the person and work of Jesus. It is near because the King has come; it advances as His word heals, delivers, and gathers a people.

pisteuo.gloss: To believe, trust, rely on. Jesus pairs it with repentance as the fitting response to the good news: not mere agreement but a wholehearted turning to God and resting in His promise in Christ.

exousia.gloss: Authority, right, power to act. The crowds marvel that Jesus teaches with authority unlike the scribes, and that even unclean spirits obey Him. His authority is inherent, not borrowed, the authority of God's own King.

katharizo.gloss: To cleanse, make clean, purify. Leprosy made a person ceremonially unclean and cut off from the community. Jesus does not become unclean by touching the leper; instead His touch makes the unclean clean, a sign of the deeper cleansing He brings.

splanchnizomai.gloss: To be moved with compassion, from the word for the inward parts; a gut-deep mercy. Jesus is stirred to the depths at the leper's plight and reaches out to touch the untouchable, showing the heart of God toward the outcast.

basic.context: John has been arrested, and Jesus steps into the open with His first sermon: the time has come, God's kingdom is near, so repent and believe. He calls four fishermen who drop everything to follow. In Capernaum He teaches with an authority that stuns everyone and casts out an unclean spirit. He heals Peter's mother-in-law and then a whole town at the door. Before dawn He slips away to pray, then presses on to preach elsewhere. Finally He touches and cleanses a leper, the untouchable outcast, moved with deep compassion.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as a display of what it means that the kingdom is near: the King's word carries authority over disciples, demons, disease, and defilement. Each scene answers the question of who Jesus is. Notice too the rhythm of power and prayer, and Jesus' insistence that His mission is to preach, not merely to draw crowds.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus preaches the euangelion, the good news, that the basileia, the kingdom of God, has drawn near, calling people to repent and pisteuo, believe. He teaches with exousia, authority, that astonishes. Moved with splanchnizomai, gut-deep compassion, He touches a leper and speaks katharizo, be clean.
basic.typology: Jesus cleansing the leper with a touch reverses the flow of defilement: under the law the clean became unclean by contact, but here the unclean is made clean. It anticipates the greater cleansing from sin He brings, and shows Him as the true priest who heals rather than merely diagnoses.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Holy One of God, as even the demon confesses. He is the King who announces the kingdom, the authoritative teacher, the stronger One who commands demons, the healer, and the compassionate cleanser of the outcast. His authority is His own, not borrowed.
basic.god: The good news is the good news of God: His reign, His initiative, His rescue. God draws near in Jesus with power and compassion, healing bodies and confronting evil, and calls people to turn to Him.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 52 announces the good news of God's reign. Leviticus 13 and 14 give the law of the leper Jesus fulfils. Matthew 4 parallels the calling of the disciples.
basic.oneStory: The kingdom promised through the prophets arrives in Jesus. He gathers the first of a new people, defeats the powers that oppress, heals the broken, and cleanses the outcast, all signs that God's saving reign has broken in. The right response then and now is the same: repent and believe the good news.

context.literary:
Mark 1:14 to 45 is built as a sequence of short scenes joined by the word 'immediately' and its relatives, so that the reader feels the speed of a single day and its aftermath. The summary of verses 14 and 15 acts as the headline, and the five scenes that follow are the proof. There is a pleasing symmetry. Jesus calls two pairs of brothers, verses 16 to 20, and the next scenes show what the call is for: He teaches, He commands, He heals, He prays and moves on, and He touches one more outcast. The passage opens with a summons to a crowd and ends with a single man begging on his knees, so the kingdom comes to the many and to the one.

The Capernaum scenes of verses 21 to 34 form a tight unit, running from Sabbath morning to evening. A synagogue exorcism, a healing in a house, and a crowd at the door cover three places in one day. Mark frames the unit with teaching, 'taught as one who had authority', verse 22, and with the news going out, verse 28. The reaction in verse 27, 'A new teaching with authority!', joins the word and the deed. The reader is meant to see that the exorcism is itself a form of the teaching.

Verses 35 to 39 are a hinge. After the full day Jesus withdraws to pray and then redirects the mission. It is the first of several scenes in Mark that show Jesus in prayer, and it sets a pattern: public power rests on private communion. Finally the leper, verses 40 to 45, ends the chapter with a pair of surprising reversals. The cleansed man is told to be silent and speaks, and Jesus, the one who touched the unclean, is the one who ends up outside the towns in the places where lepers lived. The outcast is brought in and the healer goes out.
context.historical:
Capernaum was a lakeside town on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, on a main road, with a fishing economy and a customs station. It was the base for Jesus' Galilean ministry and the home of Simon and Andrew, Mark 1:29. The synagogue where He taught would have been the centre of town life, a place where the Law was read and expounded on the Sabbath by whoever the leaders invited. A visiting teacher might be asked to speak, which explains how Jesus could enter the synagogue on the Sabbath and begin to teach, verse 21. The scribes whom the crowds compare Him with were the trained interpreters of the Law, and they normally taught by citing earlier authorities. A teacher who spoke in his own right, 'But I tell you', as Jesus does, would have been astonishing, Matthew 7:28 to 29.

The fishermen of verses 16 to 20 were small business owners, not poor peasants. James and John had hired men, verse 20, and a family boat. The call asks them to give up a trade and a household. In a society where sons followed fathers into the family work, leaving a father in the boat was costly, and it explains why the call is recorded so briefly and so sharply.

The leper in verse 40 would have lived under the regulations of Leviticus 13 and 14. The BSB footnote notes that 'leprosy' here is a word for a range of skin diseases. A person so affected 'must live alone in a place outside the camp', Leviticus 13:46, and cry out 'Unclean, unclean!' To approach Jesus, kneel and ask was a daring breach of the rules. The command to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded, verse 44, follows Leviticus 14:2 to 4, which describes the ritual of cleansing. The unclean spirits were also understood to be a source of defilement, which is why Mark calls the first one 'unclean', verse 23, a word that links the exorcism and the leper scene.
context.canonical:
The opening announcement of the kingdom draws on the prophets' hope. Isaiah 52:7 speaks of the messenger on the mountains who brings good news and says to Zion, 'Your God reigns!' Daniel had seen that 'the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed', Daniel 2:44, and had been shown the saints receiving the sovereignty, Daniel 7:27. When Jesus says that the time is fulfilled and the kingdom is near, He declares that these promises have reached their moment.

The call of the fishermen echoes the call of Elisha, who left his oxen and followed Elijah, 1 Kings 19:19 to 21, and also the prophets' use of the image of fishermen. Jeremiah 16:16 speaks of God sending many fishermen to catch people for judgment, and Ezekiel 47:10 sees fishermen standing by a healed sea. Jesus' variation, 'fishers of men', gathers people for rescue. The teaching with authority recalls Moses' promise that God would raise up a prophet like him, Deuteronomy 18:15, though Mark treats Jesus as greater than a prophet.

The healings are taken by Matthew as fulfilment of Isaiah 53:4, 'He took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows', Matthew 8:16 to 17, which relates these healings to the Servant's work. Isaiah 35:5 to 6 had promised the opening of blind eyes and the leaping of the lame in the day of God's coming. The cleansing of the leper reaches back to the law of Leviticus 13 and 14 and to the story of Naaman, the foreign commander cleansed in the Jordan, 2 Kings 5:1 to 14. It reaches forward to Luke's report that Jesus says He 'must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well', Luke 4:43, and to the church's mission in Acts. The theme of the Holy One of God returns in Peter's confession, John 6:69.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wants his readers to see that the nearness of God's reign is not a general idea but a person acting, and he builds the chapter to answer a single question, who is this? The reader sees the answer progressively. A voice from heaven told us in chapter 1, and now the human witnesses react in puzzlement. The crowd asks, 'What is this?', verse 27. The demons know exactly who He is. The disciples know only that everyone is looking for Him, verse 37. Mark keeps the reader one step ahead and invites them to see what the characters do not yet see.

He also wants readers to feel the force of the demand in verse 15. The kingdom is not only a thing to admire. It calls for repentance and belief, and the first four disciples show what that looks like: they leave their nets at once. The rest of the chapter shows why they were right to follow, for the person who calls them is the one who commands unclean spirits, raises the sick and touches the leper.

Mark has one more purpose, which is to warn against misunderstanding. The crowds want healing and miracles. Jesus will not be reduced to that, which is why He leaves for other towns, verses 38 to 39, and why He asks for silence. Mark is shaping readers who will follow Him all the way to the cross, not those who merely enjoy the signs.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter narrates what Jesus did in a particular place and day, and most of it is not a command to be copied. The exorcisms, the healings and the touching of the leper describe the work of the one with unique authority. Believers are not told to expect to repeat these things on the same terms, and nobody should read this passage as a promise that every illness will be healed. What it shows is the character of the King and the coming of His kingdom.

A few things are prescriptive in the plainest sense. Verse 15 is a call addressed to all hearers: repent and believe. The call to follow in verse 17 is the pattern of discipleship, though how it is lived varies, and not everyone is asked to leave a trade. The record of Jesus praying before daybreak, verse 35, is an example that disciples are meant to take seriously. And Jesus' instruction to the leper to show himself to the priest honours the law of Moses, which does not mean it prescribes that practice for us, since the sacrificial system has been fulfilled in Christ. The leper's disobedience in verse 45 is recorded, not commended. The chapter is honest about the cost: the man's good news meant that Jesus could no longer enter a town openly.

debates.question: Was Jesus 'moved with compassion' or angry when He touched the leper?

views.label: Compassion
views.case: Most manuscripts and the BSB text say Jesus was moved with compassion, the Greek splanchnizomai, a word used of Jesus in the Gospels for deep pity. The tenderness of the touch and the words 'I am willing' fit that reading, and the same verb marks other healings, as in Mark 6:34 and 8:2.

views.label: Indignation
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that some manuscripts have 'moved with indignation' in verse 41. Some scholars argue that this is the harder reading and thus the more likely original, since a copyist would more easily change anger to compassion than the reverse. Mark elsewhere shows Jesus angry, as in Mark 3:5, and the verb in verse 43 for the stern warning has an emotional edge. On this view Jesus is angry at the disease, at the way it isolates people, and at the power behind it.

debates.bearing: Either reading keeps the scene intact. If the original is compassion, Jesus' heart goes out to the man; if it is indignation, His anger is directed at the ruin that sin and sickness have brought, not at the sufferer. Both say that Jesus enters the man's misery and acts. What should not be done is to read the passage as if Jesus were angry at the man for asking.

debates.question: What does 'that is why I have come' refer to in verse 38?

views.label: He came out from Capernaum
views.case: The Greek says 'for this I came out' and may simply refer to leaving the town of Capernaum, verse 38, on the way to preach elsewhere. The context supports a simple reading, since Simon and the others had come to find Him and Jesus is moving on.

views.label: He was sent by the Father
views.case: Luke gives the same saying as 'because that is why I was sent', Luke 4:43, and so many take the 'coming out' in Mark as a statement about His mission from God. Preaching, and not only healing, is what He was sent to do. The reading fits the way Mark begins with the Father's voice and the Spirit's sending in 1:9 to 13.

debates.bearing: The two readings can both be true: He left the house to go to other towns because that is what the Father sent Him to do. Whichever sense is primary, the point is that Jesus will not let the crowd's demand for healing set His agenda. His mission is to proclaim the kingdom, and the healings are signs of it.

study.originalLanguages:
In verse 15 'the time is fulfilled' is peplerotai ho kairos. The word is kairos, not chronos. Chronos is time that passes on the clock; kairos is an appointed moment, a season ripe for something. The verb is in the perfect tense, which describes a completed action whose result stands. The time has been filled up and now stands full. The next clause, 'the kingdom of God is near', uses eggiken, also perfect, 'has drawn near'. Both clauses say that something has already happened: God's reign has arrived at the edge of the present and is pressing in. The two commands, 'repent' and 'believe', are both present imperatives, which gives them the sense of a settled direction of life and not a single decision. And the construction 'believe in the gospel' is unusual, since believing is more often directed at a person. It suggests that the good news is itself the object of trust.

The call of the fishermen has Jesus say 'Come, follow Me', deute opiso mou, literally 'come after me' or 'come behind me'. The phrase is the language of a disciple who walks behind his teacher, and it is more demanding than an invitation to listen. 'Fishers of men', halieis anthropon, takes their trade and redirects it. The verbs of their response are immediate and physical. They 'left' their nets and followed, and the second pair left their father in the boat.

In the synagogue, the demon's words begin with an idiom that is difficult to translate, ti hemin kai soi, literally 'what to us and to you?' The phrase appears in the Greek Old Testament, as in 1 Kings 17:18, and means roughly 'what do we have in common?' or 'leave us alone'. The speaker shifts between 'us' and 'I', as though the man and the spirit speak together. Jesus' command to the spirit, 'Be silent', is the verb phimoo, which means 'to muzzle'. Mark uses it again when Jesus commands the wind and the sea in Mark 4:39. The same word of power tames a demon and a storm. The shriek of the spirit 'came out', and the crowd's phrase 'a new teaching with authority' ties the new teaching to the authority that has just been displayed.

The healing of Peter's mother-in-law uses language that goes further than it first seems. Jesus 'took her by the hand and helped her up', and the verb for 'raised' is egeiro, the verb Mark uses of resurrection, as in Mark 16:6. She then 'served' them, diakoneo, the same verb used of the angels in Mark 1:13 and later of the Son of Man in Mark 10:45. It was ordinary service, but Mark's choice of words lets the reader see that being raised by Jesus leads to serving.

In the leper scene Jesus 'reached out His hand and touched', hapsamenos, 'taking hold of' the man, and says thelo, 'I am willing'. The man had said 'If You are willing', and Jesus answers in the same word, so the will of Jesus matches the man's request. Then Mark says Jesus 'sent him away with a stern warning', using embrimaomai, a word of strong feeling, and the verb for 'sent away' is ekballo, 'cast out', the very verb used for expelling demons and for the Spirit's driving of Jesus into the wilderness in Mark 1:12. The strong language shows that the instruction to be silent was urgent and that the man's later disobedience was a real fault.

typology.fulfillment: Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha, who was ploughing, and Elisha left his oxen, slaughtered them for a farewell meal, and followed. The pattern of a prophet's call, a trade abandoned, and a master followed is repeated in Mark 1:16 to 20. Jesus does more than Elijah, for He does not throw a cloak over His chosen ones but speaks with divine authority, and He gives no time for a farewell. Elijah's call carried the prophet's authority; Jesus' call carries the authority of the Lord. The correspondence is in the pattern of immediate, costly following, and the escalation is in the person called to follow, who is not a prophet but the One the prophets announced.

typology.type: Naaman and the cleansing of the leper, 2 Kings 5
typology.fulfillment: The king of Israel despaired when the Aramean general came for healing, 'Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper?' 2 Kings 5:7. The cure came through Elisha's word and the Jordan's water. In Mark 1 a leper comes to Jesus, and Jesus cures him with a touch and a word, and without any washing. The earlier story showed that cleansing of leprosy was God's work alone, and in Jesus the same work is done directly. The type has a limit: Naaman was a foreigner who came to the prophet, and the leper in Mark is presumably an Israelite who has to be sent to the priest, which shows that Jesus is both greater than the prophet and respectful of the law.

typology.type: The servant who carries our sickness, Isaiah 53:4
typology.fulfillment: Matthew says that the healings of the Capernaum evening fulfilled the word of Isaiah, 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases', Matthew 8:16 to 17. Mark gives the same evening without quoting the prophet, but the picture is the same: the sick are brought, and the healer takes their burden on Himself. The fullest sense is found at the cross, where the Servant 'bore the sin of many', Isaiah 53:12, and the healings are early signs of it. The type is still unfolding, since bodily healing in this age is partial and sin and death are only finally dealt with in the new creation.

typology.type: The desert place and the prayer of the Lord
typology.fulfillment: Jesus goes at dawn to a 'solitary place', from the same root as the wilderness of Mark 1:12 and 1:13. He returns to the place of testing but now to pray, and the earlier solitude of the wilderness is a place where the Father's voice and the angels' care were known. The scene links the Son's praying with the Spirit who drove Him out. It is a pattern more than a type: the one who is always heard by the Father shows what a life of prayer looks like, and Luke 5:16 says He often did it. It falls short as a precise prefiguring, since no Old Testament figure is its single pattern, but it fits the many who sought God in the wilderness.

study.christ:
Mark 1:14 to 45 shows Christ by showing what the kingdom does when it arrives. He is first the herald and the king at once. The good news He proclaims is the 'gospel of God', verse 14, and yet the news is also about Him. In the next verses He speaks of the kingdom as near because He is near. The Old Testament had said, 'Your God reigns!' Isaiah 52:7, and now the reign of God is a man walking beside a lake and calling fishermen.

He is the one with a unique authority. The crowd's astonishment is that He teaches 'as one who had authority, and not as the scribes', verse 22. The scribes cited others; Jesus speaks in His own name. Then the same authority shows itself over demons. The spirit's cry, 'the Holy One of God', is a confession wrung from an enemy, and it points to a holiness that does not shrink from uncleanness but overcomes it. Mark's demons know who He is and Jesus silences them, verse 34, because the time for the open declaration has not yet come. He is also the stronger one who will, as Mark 3:27 says, tie up the strong man, the first step in a conflict that runs to the cross.

He is the compassionate healer who takes our burdens. When Peter's mother-in-law is raised and the whole town gathers at the door, the pattern is of One who bears what He heals. Matthew explains it with Isaiah 53:4, that He 'took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows', and the New Testament sees that taking-on in the cross. At the leper's request He answers, 'I am willing', and He touches. A leper made others unclean by contact, but here Jesus is not made unclean; the cleanness flows from Him to the leper. The touch is a picture of the gospel in miniature. The One who is holy comes close to the unclean and makes them clean. At the cross He would take on the uncleanness itself, which is why the final result of this touching is that He is driven to live in desolate places, as the leper had.

He is a man of prayer. The Son who has authority over demons and disease goes before dawn to speak with the Father. This does not weaken His authority; it shows its source and relation. He lives as a Son who depends on the Father, and He refuses to be kept by the crowd. His reply to Simon, 'for that is why I have come', shows that He knows His purpose.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The details of this chapter should not be turned into allegory. The fishing nets are not a code for the law, the fever is not a symbol of sin, and Capernaum is not a figure for the church. The links to Christ are established by what the text says plainly: His authority, His mercy, His holiness, His prayer and His sense of mission.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that He acts in history in His own time. 'The time is fulfilled', verse 15, says that God has had an appointed moment in mind and that it has arrived. The long wait of Israel and the silence of the prophets were not the absence of God but the preparation of a moment. God is the Lord of kairos as well as of eternity, and He keeps His appointments.

The passage shows God as a king who comes near. 'Near' is the keyword, and the Old Testament had often pictured God as distant, enthroned on a mountain, behind a veil. Here He comes into synagogues and houses and onto a lakeside. The kingdom is not an idea but the reign of the living God pressing into the world of fishermen and fevers. Isaiah's cry of 'Your God reigns!' is answered in places as ordinary as a kitchen where a fever leaves a woman.

It shows God as holy and as merciful at once. The unclean spirit cries out, 'the Holy One of God'. The same holiness that terrifies demons draws the leper. The law of Leviticus kept the unclean outside the camp so that God's holiness would not be profaned, Numbers 5:3. In Jesus the holiness is shown to be stronger than the uncleanness, and the touch that would have defiled any other man becomes the means of cleansing. The same God who is 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger', Exodus 34:6, is revealed in the Lord who stretches out His hand.

It shows God as the one who wars against evil. The demons are real, they know who Jesus is, and Jesus has authority to command them. Evil is not neutral or imaginary, and it is not equal to God. The same word of power that silences a demon calms the sea in Mark 4:39, and the God of Psalm 107:29 who 'calmed the storm to a whisper' is the one whose word is on the lips of Jesus. The presence of the kingdom means that the realm of evil is being taken from the inside.

Finally, the passage shows a God who calls people to Himself. 'Repent and believe' is the invitation of a God who wants to be known and trusted. The disciples are not dragged but called. For worship, the passage invites a response like the leper's, who comes to Jesus on his knees and says, 'If You are willing'. It also teaches a restraint in worship: that Jesus withdraws to pray shows that even the Son seeks the Father, and the church's worship rests on the same dependence.

crossReferences.note: The messenger on the mountains proclaims peace and salvation and says to Zion, 'Your God reigns!' Mark's description of Jesus proclaiming the gospel of God draws on this passage and presents the kingdom as the arrival of God's reign promised by Isaiah.

God will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed. Jesus' announcement that the kingdom of God is near stands in the line of Daniel's vision of a kingdom that outlasts all earthly powers, and it explains why His claim touches every sphere of life.

Elijah calls Elisha from the plough, and Elisha leaves his oxen to follow. The pattern of a prophet's call, immediate and costly, is the background to Jesus calling fishermen from their nets, though the authority of Jesus' call is far greater.

God says He will send for many fishermen to catch His people for judgment. Jesus' 'fishers of men' takes up the image of fishing and turns it toward gathering and rescue. It shows that He chooses a familiar image and transforms its meaning.

Matthew places the same evening of healings and quotes Isaiah: 'He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases.' It shows how the early church read these healings, as the first signs of the Servant who bears the burdens of His people.

The unclean, including those with skin disease, were to be sent outside the camp 'so they will not defile their camp, where I dwell among them.' The law protected God's holy presence. Jesus' touch of the leper shows a holiness that cleanses instead of being contaminated.

The law of cleansing describes the priest going outside the camp to examine the healed person and the offerings to be brought. Jesus tells the man to follow it in Mark 1:44, so that the priests, as the verse says, receive a testimony to what has happened.

The king of Israel asks, 'Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper?' The question shows that only God could heal leprosy. Jesus heals it with a word and a touch, and so acts as God in the sight of onlookers.

Jesus says He must preach the good news of the kingdom to other towns 'because that is why I was sent'. It parallels Mark 1:38 and clarifies that His coming is a sending by the Father, with preaching at the centre of His mission.

No one can enter a strong man's house unless he first ties up the strong man. The exorcism in the synagogue is the first sign of this conflict. Jesus is already at work taking the house of the powers that hold people.

The Son of Man came 'not to be served, but to serve'. The verb for service in Mark 1:31, where Peter's mother-in-law serves, is the same verb as in this verse. The chapter's small acts of serving look forward to His great act of giving His life.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward the Bible shows a world where sin has brought sickness, uncleanness, exile and the rule of evil powers. The promise of Genesis 3:15 was that a descendant would one day crush the serpent. Through the law, the prophets and the exile God's people learned how deep the trouble ran, and the prophets kept saying that God Himself would come and reign. Isaiah heard a messenger say, 'Your God reigns!' and Daniel saw an everlasting kingdom set up by the God of heaven.

Mark 1:14 to 45 is the moment when the announcement begins to be true. The kingdom of God is near, and Mark shows it in action at once. Fishermen become the first of a new people, a gathering that will become the church. A demon is silenced in a synagogue, and the territory the powers had held is invaded. The sick are healed, which the prophets had said would mark the day of God's coming, Isaiah 35:5 to 6. A leper, the very picture of exclusion from God's camp, is touched and made clean. In a few verses the effects of the fall that Genesis described, uncleanness, illness and bondage, are being turned back.

The passage also looks ahead. The healing of Peter's mother-in-law, the cry of the demon, the shadow of the leper's isolation and the pressure of the crowds all point to what is coming in Mark's story. Jesus will be the Holy One who bears uncleanness instead of avoiding it, the one who 'took on our infirmities', Isaiah 53:4, at the cross. His withdrawal to solitary places and His insistence on preaching show that His mission is not primarily to relieve symptoms but to bring the reign of God into the lives of those who repent and believe. The healings are signs; the cross is the means.

The story continues in the church. The disciples who left their nets are sent out to fish for people, Matthew 28:19 and Acts 1:8. The authority of Jesus over evil is carried forward by His Spirit, and the gospel of the kingdom is proclaimed to the nations, Matthew 24:14.

The end of the story is the new creation, where the sick are healed fully and the unclean are no more. John sees the city in which God dwells with His people and wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:3 to 4. Every healing in Mark 1 is a small pledge of that world, and every call to repent and believe is an invitation to belong to it.

quiz.q: What is the heart of Jesus' opening proclamation in Galilee?

options.text: The time is fulfilled and God's kingdom is near, so repent and believe the good news.
options.note: Mark 1:15 gives Jesus' own summary message.

options.text: The kingdom of God is near, so get ready for it.
options.note: Right about the kingdom's nearness, but it omits the double call to repent and believe that Jesus attaches.

options.text: People must keep the law more carefully to earn God's favour.
options.note: Jesus calls for repentance and faith in response to grace arriving, not law-keeping to earn favour.

options.text: Israel should prepare to overthrow Rome.
options.note: Jesus announces the reign of God, not a political revolt.

quiz.q: How did the first disciples respond to Jesus' call?

options.text: They left their nets and their father at once and followed Him.
options.note: Mark 1:18 and 1:20 show their immediate, wholehearted response.

options.text: They followed Him but kept fishing part-time.
options.note: They did become fishers of men, but Mark stresses they left everything at once, not a part-time arrangement.

options.text: They asked for time to consider before deciding.
options.note: The text emphasizes immediacy; they did not delay to deliberate.

options.text: They refused until Jesus performed a miracle.
options.note: They followed at His word, before any miracle was demanded.

quiz.q: Why were the people astonished at Jesus in the Capernaum synagogue?

options.text: He taught with authority, unlike the scribes, and even unclean spirits obeyed His command.
options.note: Mark 1:22 and 1:27 tie their amazement to His authority in word and over demons.

options.text: He quoted the scribes and rabbis more skillfully than others.
options.note: The opposite: His authority was unlike the scribes, inherent rather than derived from citing others.

options.text: He performed clever tricks to entertain the crowd.
options.note: His works were real acts of authority and mercy, not entertainment.

options.text: He said nothing remarkable at all.
options.note: Mark says the crowd was amazed at His authoritative teaching.

quiz.q: What does Jesus' touching and cleansing of the leper reveal?

options.text: His deep compassion and His power to make the unclean clean rather than being defiled Himself.
options.note: Moved with compassion, Jesus touches the untouchable and cleanses him, Mark 1:41-42.

options.text: That Jesus cared about people's physical suffering.
options.note: True but partial; it also reveals His authority to reverse uncleanness and picture cleansing from sin.

options.text: That Jesus was willing to break the law of Moses.
options.note: Jesus actually upholds the law, sending the man to the priest per Leviticus 14; the deeper point is His cleansing power.

options.text: That leprosy was not really a serious condition.
options.note: Leprosy meant exclusion and defilement; Jesus' act is significant precisely because the condition was grave.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus leave the crowds to pray and then move on to other towns?

options.text: His mission was to preach the good news widely, so He would not be held by one town's demand for miracles.
options.note: Mark 1:38, that is why I have come, shows His priority on preaching beyond Capernaum.

options.text: He wanted time alone with the Father before more ministry.
options.note: True, He withdrew to pray, but His stated reason for moving on was to preach in other towns.

options.text: He was tired of the people of Capernaum.
options.note: It was mission priority, not weariness with the people, that moved Him on.

options.text: He had failed to help anyone in Capernaum.
options.note: He had healed many; He moved on to extend, not because of failure.

questions: Jesus' first word is repent and believe. What would genuine repentance and fresh trust look like in your life this week?
The fishermen left their nets at once. What might Jesus be asking you to leave or reorder in order to follow Him more fully?
Even the demons could not stand against Jesus' word. How does His authority over the powers of darkness give you confidence in your own struggles?
Jesus rose before dawn to pray, even with a town clamouring for Him. How is the rhythm of your life shaped by time alone with God?
Jesus was moved with compassion and touched the untouchable. Who are the outcasts near you that His compassion would have you reach toward?

translationNotes.note: Some manuscripts read the gospel of the kingdom of God; the shorter reading, the gospel of God, is well supported and means the same good news of God's reign.
A few manuscripts read moved with indignation rather than moved with compassion; the compassion reading is widely attested and fits the tender act of touching the leper.
The demon's words, I know who You are, the Holy One of God, are an unwilling but true confession of Jesus' identity.
